think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 42-year-old nulliparous immigrant female presents with 6 months of abdominal distension, ascites, constitutional symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, omental nodularity, an ovarian cyst, and a strikingly elevated serum CA-125 level (1289 U/mL). The presentation mimicked advanced epithelial ovarian cancer with peritoneal carcinomatosis. The diagnostic tension centers on differentiating gynecologic malignancy from peritoneal tuberculosis, particularly given that peritoneal fluid cytology, acid-fast stains, and initial mycobacterial cultures and NAAT are frequently paucibacillary and negative.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint concludes after the outpatient clinical history, occupational history, physical examination, baseline laboratory investigations (normal CBC and metabolic panel, negative HIV), serum CA-125 measurement, and baseline abdominopelvic CT and transvaginal ultrasound, strictly prior to paracentesis cytology, endometrial/omental biopsies, diagnostic laparoscopy, chest CT, QuantiFERON/PPD testing, and anti-tuberculosis therapy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Advanced ovarian cancer was the primary suspicion due to marked CA-125 elevation, omental caking, ascites, and an adnexal mass, but was ruled out by benign paracentesis cytology, normal ovaries on diagnostic laparoscopy, and lack of neoplastic cells on omental biopsies. Non-infectious granulomatous peritonitis was ruled out by the demonstration of necrotizing granulomas, apical pleural scarring on chest imaging, positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus, and rapid complete clinical/radiological resolution following anti-tuberculosis therapy.
case_prompt:
A 42-year-old nulliparous woman is referred to the gynecologic oncology clinic for evaluation of progressive abdominal distension and constitutional symptoms concerning for ovarian malignancy. She reports a 6-month history of abdominal discomfort, progressive abdominal swelling, drenching night sweats, intermittent fevers, and unintentional weight loss. Her past gynecologic history includes a ruptured ovarian cyst five years prior. She was born in Brazil, where she had worked in a public health outpatient clinic providing care for chronic communicable respiratory diseases, before immigrating to the United States three years ago. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications.

On physical examination, the patient is well-appearing. Vital signs are normal. The abdomen is distended but soft, nontender, and without focal guarding. Pelvic examination demonstrates normal external genitalia, vagina, and cervix, with the uterus and cervix deviated toward the right; rectovaginal examination is unremarkable. There is no peripheral lymphadenopathy and no lower extremity edema. Heart and lung examinations are normal.

Triage laboratory evaluation reveals a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Serological testing for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies is nonreactive. Serum CA-125 is markedly elevated at 1,289 U/mL (reference <= 38.1 U/mL).

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrates moderate-volume free peritoneal fluid, diffuse nodularity throughout the greater omentum, enlarged right retroperitoneal lymph nodes measuring up to 1.4 cm, and a bilobed right ovarian cyst measuring 6.5 cm in maximal diameter. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows a hypoechoic cystic structure with low-level internal reticular echoes in the right ovary consistent with a hemorrhagic cyst, an 0.8-cm hypoechoic endometrial focus, and myometrial cystic changes.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered the primary provisional diagnosis given the combination of massive CA-125 elevation (1,289 U/mL), omental nodularity ('omental caking'), ascites, and an adnexal mass; however, paracentesis fluid cytology showed only benign mesothelial cells, endometrial and omental biopsies showed no neoplasm, and diagnostic laparoscopy confirmed normal ovaries without malignant lesions.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A 42-year-old G0 female was referred to the gynecology oncology outpatient clinic for evaluation of symptoms and imaging findings concerning for ovarian cancer... Paracentesis was performed and showed rare benign mesothelial cells. Endometrial biopsy showed secretory endometrium without evidence of malignant cells. A CT-guided omental biopsy showed granulomas without evidence of neoplasm

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Non-Infectious Granulomatous Peritonitis (e.g., Sarcoidosis, Ruptured Cyst Reaction)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered upon discovery of omental granulomas without malignant cells; however, the presence of necrotizing (caseating) granulomas, chest CT showing biapical pleural scarring and a parenchymal nodule, a 10-mm tuberculin skin test, and a positive interferon-gamma release assay identified an infectious etiology.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Pathology of the omental and abdominal wall biopsies showed benign fibroadipose tissue with necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomas but without acid fast bacilli seen on modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining... CT of the chest showed a 4 mm left lower lobe nodule and biapical mild pleural parenchymal scarring. A tuberculin skin test showed 10 mm induration, and a blood QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus interferon-gamma release assay (Qiagen) was positive.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot occurred when laparoscopic biopsy demonstrated necrotizing granulomas, alongside positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus and remote apical lung scarring; empirical quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy led to rapid clinical recovery, CA-125 reduction to 74 U/mL at 4 weeks, and complete radiological resolution of omental caking, ascites, and lymphadenopathy at 8 weeks.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Due to concern for peritoneal tuberculosis, treatment was initiated with isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Within four weeks of treatment, the CA-125 had decreased to 74 U/mL, and she had substantial clinical improvement including resolution of fevers, reduction in abdominal discomfort, increased appetite, and weight gain. At eight weeks after tuberculosis treatment initiation, her abdominal pain was entirely resolved... and CT abdomen and pelvis showed resolution of omental caking, ascites, and lymphadenopathy.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly per Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. The admission prompt omits disease/pathogen names, capturing the diagnostic mimicry between peritoneal tuberculosis and ovarian carcinomatosis.
